recK8YDQPDlhk05Me.label: Yarn
recK8YDQPDlhk05Me.body: Found only in [1 Kings 10:28](/1kgs#1Kgs.10.28), [2](/1kgs#1Kgs.10.2) Chr. 1:16. The Heb. word mikveh, i.e., “a stringing together,” so rendered, rather signifies a host, or company, or a string of horses. The Authorized Version has: “And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn: the king’s merchants received the linen yarn at a price;” but the Revised Version correctly renders: “And the horses which Solomon had were brought out of Egypt; the king’s merchants received them in droves, each drove at a price.”

recoCmvm9iaDW1epQ.label: Year
recoCmvm9iaDW1epQ.body: Heb. shanah, meaning “repetition” or “revolution” ([Gen. 1:14](/gen#Gen.1.14); [5:3](/gen#Gen.5.3)). Among the ancient Egyptians the year consisted of twelve months of thirty days each, with five days added to make it a complete revolution of the earth round the sun. The Jews reckoned the year in two ways, (1) according to a sacred calendar, in which the year began about the time of the vernal equinox, with the month Abib; and (2) according to a civil calendar, in which the year began about the time of the autumnal equinox, with the month Nisan. The month Tisri is now the beginning of the Jewish year.

rec74ePEy55LG10jt.label: Yeshebi
rec74ePEy55LG10jt.body: The Hebrew word rendered “inhabitants” in [Josh. 17:7](/josh#Josh.17.7), but probably rather the name of the village Yeshepheh, probably Yassuf, 8 miles south of Shechem.

rechBjBdK1IShYccM.label: Yoke
rechBjBdK1IShYccM.body: Fitted on the neck of oxen for the purpose of binding to them the traces by which they might draw the plough, etc. ([Num. 19:2](/num#Num.19.2); [Deut. 21:3](/deut#Deut.21.3)). It was a curved piece of wood called ’ol.

recfV1vMapxXHP0rR.label: Yoke
recfV1vMapxXHP0rR.body:
In [Jer. 27:2](/jer#Jer.27.2); [28:10](/jer#Jer.28.10), [12](/jer#Jer.28.12) the word in the Authorized Version rendered “yoke” is motah, which properly means a “staff,” or as in the Revised Version, “bar.”

 These words in the Hebrew are both used figuratively of severe bondage, or affliction, or subjection ([Lev. 26:13](/lev#Lev.26.13); [1 Kings 12:4](/1kgs#1Kgs.12.4); [Isa. 47:6](/isa#Isa.47.6); [Lam. 1:14](/lam#Lam.1.14); [3:27](/lam#Lam.3.27)). In the New Testament the word “yoke” is also used to denote servitude ([Matt. 11:29](/matt#Matt.11.29), [30](/matt#Matt.11.30); [Acts 15:10](/acts#Acts.15.10); [Gal. 5:1](/gal#Gal.5.1)).

recS252KeWl7bTInI.label: Yoke
recS252KeWl7bTInI.body: In [1 Sam. 11:7](/1sam#1Sam.11.7), [1](/1sam#1Sam.11.1) Kings 19:21, [Job 1:3](/job#Job.1.3) the word thus translated is tzemed, which signifies a pair, two oxen yoked or coupled together, and hence in [1 Sam. 14:14](/1sam#1Sam.14.14) it represents as much land as a yoke of oxen could plough in a day, like the Latin jugum. In [Isa. 5:10](/isa#Isa.5.10) this word in the plural is translated “acres.”

rec7cD0gofDYTCx1W.label: Yoke-fellow
rec7cD0gofDYTCx1W.body: ([Phil. 4:3](/phil#Phil.4.3)), one of the apostle’s fellow-labourers. Some have conjectured that Epaphroditus is meant. Wyckliffe renders the phrase “the german felowe”, i.e., “thee, germane [=genuine] comrade.”
